To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The use of technology in educational settings, and the increased focus on web accessibility, are connected to neo-liberla agendas within higher education, and the delivery of instruction online positions teachers and learners in particular discursive formations.
web accessibility, while well-intentioned, is often used in ways that reinforce the very social and epistemological inequalities that accessibility was intended to ameliorate.
the use of distance education technology and the application of web accessibility standards are not neutral in terms of the construction of knowledge and learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways in which the increasing technologization of instruction is linked to the commodification of education and the ways in which web accessibility standards, as they are articulated with other discursive formations (such as neo-liberalism), are implicated in the construction of particular knowledge and learning styles.
the ways in which web accessibility is connected to the commodification of knowledge and the ways in which this commodification of knowledge impacts the lives of learners with disabilities.
the ways that technology mediates instruction and the ways that this mediation is linked to broader ideological and epistemological shifts within higher education.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the commodification of education and the commodification of the body (and the body politic) are inextricably linked.
web accessibility is not a neutral or value-free endeavor, but one that is deeply implicated in the construction of knowledge.
web accessibility is a technology of power and that it mediates the production and consumption of knowledge in ways that reflect particular epistemologies and ideologies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
web accessibility, while a laudable goal, is often used to further commodify educational processes.

the use of technology within education, including the use of distance learning technology and web accessibility, is a site of struggle over the construction of knowledge, the production of subjects, and the commodification of education.
web accessibility standards are increasingly connected to the commodification of education and the construction of disability as a marketable condition.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the increasing technologizing and marketization of education is not simply a matter of efficiency or convenience, but is rather a matter of ideology, epistemology, and the production of particular kinds of knowledge and subjects.
the increasing use of distance education technologies and web accessibility standards is part and parcel of a larger neo-liberal agenda in higher education.

, as the use of technology in education continues to expand, the need to critically examine the ways in which technology is being deployed and to understand the ideological implications of these practices becomes more urgent.
